answer.sourceLine: This exact wording appears in none of Milne’s books. Quote Investigator found “currently there is no substantive evidence that A. A. Milne employed this quotation,” and traces the earliest instance of this precise phrasing only to a Mount Carmel, Illinois newspaper in November 1999. source.excerpt: If you live to be a hundred, I want to live to be a hundred minus one day, so I never have to live without you.
trail: Quote Investigator concludes “currently there is no substantive evidence that A. A. Milne employed this quotation,” dating the earliest exact phrasing to a Mount Carmel, Illinois paper in November 1999.
The same investigation credits the underlying idea to Tom Phillips, whose verse ran in The Rotarian, January 1917: “May you all live forever / May I live forever less a day…”
A rare-books survey of “authentic Winnie-the-Pooh quotes” flags this as “the most widely shared” Pooh line that “was not written by Milne.”
source.excerptNote: Widely captioned as Winnie-the-Pooh or A. A. Milne — but absent from every Pooh book. The closest real Milne passage, at the end of The House at Pooh Corner, has Christopher Robin and Pooh imagine being “a hundred” and “ninety-nine” — one year apart, with no mention of never living without the other.

source.rightsNote: The exact modern wording has no identified author — it is first documented in a 1999 newspaper with no byline — so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted for it. (Tom Phillips’ 1917 Rotarian verse, a different text, would itself be public domain, but it is not this quotation.)

author.name: A. A. Milne
author.heading: The name on the caption
author.metaLine: 1882–1956 · English playwright, novelist & creator of Winnie-the-Pooh
author.bio: Alan Alexander Milne gave the world Winnie-the-Pooh (1926) and The House at Pooh Corner (1928), whose gentle prose has made him a magnet for feel-good lines he never wrote. His genuine closing scene — Christopher Robin and Pooh imagining themselves at “a hundred” and “ninety-nine” — is almost certainly the seed later reshaped, by other hands, into this ‘hundred minus one day’ internet quotation.

misattribution.heading: How Pooh got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook feel-good misattribution: a tender, quotable line pinned to a beloved gentle author who never wrote it.

items.why: The line appears in neither Winnie-the-Pooh nor The House at Pooh Corner. Quote Investigator found “no substantive evidence that A. A. Milne employed this quotation.”

items.who: The end of The House at Pooh Corner (1928)
items.why: Milne’s actual scene has the pair picture being “a hundred” and “ninety-nine” — one year apart, with no line about never having to live without each other, per QI’s comparison.
QI credits the underlying sentiment to Phillips’ verse in The Rotarian, January 1917: “May you all live forever / May I live forever less a day…” — a wholly different wording.

misattribution.truthLine: The exact ‘hundred minus one day’ phrasing is traced by Quote Investigator only to a Mount Carmel, Illinois newspaper in November 1999 — more than forty years after Milne’s death, and with no author’s name attached.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Pooh
lead: The line thrives because it feels exactly like something Pooh would say, and because Milne really did write a wistful farewell scene about a boy and a bear growing old. That genuine kernel — “a hundred” and “ninety-nine” at the close of The House at Pooh Corner — gives the fabrication just enough truth to feel remembered rather than invented.

The 1997 direct-to-video film Pooh’s Grand Adventure echoes that same ‘hundred / ninety-nine’ exchange, which is often mistaken online for the source of the ‘minus one day’ wording. But the precise quotation everyone shares is not spoken there either; the earliest documented instance of it remains the 1999 newspaper caption.
context.pull: It feels like Pooh — which is exactly why nobody checks the book.
